howToRefresh: Ingest the KY History morning email to public/content/raw-briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md, run npm run parse-briefs, then npm run build (includes build-home-preview). The homepage also re-reads stories.json in the browser.

stories.title: Father David Rice and Kentucky’s first Presbyterian churches
stories.summary: Father David Rice organized Concord Church at Danville in 1784, argued for gradual emancipation in 1792, and later preached from his home near Greensburg.
stories.place: Father David Rice home marker, Greensburg (KHS #844)
stories.quote: David Rice was about fifty years old when he crossed the mountains into Kentucky in 1783.

photo.title: First Presbyterian Church, Danville, descendant of Rice’s Concord Church (photographed 2012)
photo.attribution: Joel Bradshaw · Wikimedia Commons · CC0

stories.heroDeck: David Rice was about fifty years old when he crossed the mountains into Kentucky in 1783.

stories.title: La Grange: the Oldham County seat with trains on Main Street
stories.summary: La Grange began in 1827 at a crossroads named for Lafayette’s estate, became the Oldham County seat in 1838, and still runs trains down Main Street.
stories.place: La Grange courthouse square and Main Street tracks
stories.quote: Oldham County was cut from Jefferson, Shelby and Henry counties in the 1820s, the state’s 74th county.

photo.title: A freight train on Main Street, La Grange (photographed 2010)
photo.attribution: Morgan from Halifax, Nova Scotia · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

stories.heroDeck: Oldham County was cut from Jefferson, Shelby and Henry counties in the 1820s, the state’s 74th county.

stories.title: River Raisin, 1813: Kentucky’s winter defeat in Michigan
stories.summary: Kentucky volunteers who mustered at Georgetown in 1812 were defeated at the River Raisin in January 1813 by British troops and Wyandot-led warriors.
stories.place: Remember the Raisin: Kentucky volunteers' muster, Georgetown (KHS #508)
stories.quote: On August 15, 1812, Kentucky volunteers gathered on the courthouse square at Georgetown, ordered north to relieve Gen. William Hull at Detroit.

photo.title: River Raisin National Battlefield Park, Monroe, Michigan (photographed 2010)
photo.attribution: Notorious4life · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: On August 15, 1812, Kentucky volunteers gathered on the courthouse square at Georgetown, ordered north to relieve Gen. William Hull at Detroit.

stories.title: C. and O. Mounds: Adena Burial Mounds in Johnson County
stories.summary: In Johnson County, the C. and O. Mounds are two Adena burial mounds that William S. Webb dug and used to explain how Adena people lived.
stories.place: C. and O. Mounds, Johnson County (approximate)
stories.quote: In Johnson County, people of the Adena culture raised two burial mounds about 1,600 feet apart.

photo.title: An Adena bird effigy pipe from Ohio, Cleveland Museum of Art; a generic Adena artifact, not from the Johnson County mounds
photo.attribution: Cleveland Museum of Art · Wikimedia Commons · CC0

stories.heroDeck: In Johnson County, people of the Adena culture raised two burial mounds about 1,600 feet apart.

stories.title: The Maysville Road and Jackson’s veto, 1830
stories.summary: The Maysville Road from the Ohio to Lexington drew Andrew Jackson’s 1830 veto of federal aid, yet Kentucky finished the turnpike in 1835 on today’s US 68.
stories.quote: Long before it was a road, the way from the Ohio River at Limestone, now Maysville, to the Bluegrass was a buffalo trace that Native hunters used between the salt licks.

photo.title: “1830—The Maysville Turnpike,” illustration from the Federal Highway Administration’s America’s Highways 1776–1976
photo.attribution: Federal Highway Administration · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Long before it was a road, the way from the Ohio River at Limestone, now Maysville, to the Bluegrass was a buffalo trace that Native hunters used between the salt licks.

layers.name: Fort Boonesborough
layers.blurb: Daniel Boone’s 1775 settlement on the Kentucky River — Capital of the Colony of Transylvania.

photo.title: Fort Boonesborough reconstruction
photo.attribution: Bubba73 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Big Bone Lick
layers.blurb: A Pleistocene salt lick where mastodons left bones in the mud — Kentucky’s window on deep time.

photo.title: Big Bone Lick State Park
photo.attribution: Mattguyver · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

layers.name: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
layers.blurb: Flagship Kentucky Historical Society museum, covering more than 12,000 years of the Commonwealth.

photo.title: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
photo.attribution: Lee Wright · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

layers.name: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
layers.wiki: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park
layers.blurb: The Sinking Spring farm where Lincoln was born in 1809, plus the Knob Creek boyhood unit.

photo.title: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace memorial
photo.attribution: Jon698 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0

layers.name: Blue Licks Battlefield
layers.wiki: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
layers.blurb: August 19, 1782: the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky.

photo.title: Blue Licks Battlefield monument
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Old Talbott Tavern
layers.blurb: Court Square tavern since the late 1700s — among America’s oldest inns, still a working bourbon bar.

photo.title: Old Talbott Tavern, Bardstown
photo.attribution: Christopher L. Riley · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Goddard Covered Bridge
layers.blurb: White Bridge: a Town-lattice span over Sand Lick Creek, among Kentucky’s surviving covered bridges.

photo.title: Goddard Covered Bridge
photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Bourbon Iron Works
layers.blurb: Jacob Myers blew in a charcoal blast furnace here in 1791 — munitions for the early Commonwealth.

photo.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
photo.attribution: Jeff Bates · HABS / Library of Congress · Public domain

layers.name: The Kentucke Gazette
layers.blurb: Kentucky’s first newspaper, begun August 11, 1787 by John and Fielding Bradford.

photo.title: Kentucke Gazette printing house
photo.attribution: William Henry Perrin / Filson Club · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Cumberland Falls
layers.blurb: The “Niagara of the South,” and one of the few Western Hemisphere places a moonbow can appear.

photo.title: Cumberland Falls
photo.attribution: Aaron Vowels · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

layers.name: Frankfort Cemetery
layers.blurb: Hilltop rural cemetery (1844) overlooking the capital — Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here.

photo.title: Frankfort Cemetery
photo.attribution: Sydney Poore & Russell Poore · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Buffalo Trace Distillery
layers.blurb: A Kentucky River distilling campus with late-1700s roots, continuous through Prohibition.

photo.title: Buffalo Trace Distillery
photo.attribution: Kittugwiki · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0
